lede: Factorising runs expanding backwards: from $2x^2+9x+10$ back to the two brackets it came from. You already do it when the $x^2$ stands alone. A number in front of $x^2$ changes one thing, the pair of numbers you look for, and the rest is grouping, common factors and squares in disguise.
can: Split the middle term with a pair that multiplies to $ac$ and adds to $b$, then group.
Take out the highest common factor first, letters included, and finish every bracket.
Spot a difference of two squares in disguise: fractions, products, two letters, whole brackets.

text: Multiply to ac, add to b

alt: A two by two grid. The columns are headed 2x and +3, the rows x and +4. The cells hold 2x², +3x, +8x and +12; the corner cells 2x² and +12 are shaded.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (x + 4)(2x + 3)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+3</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+4</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x²</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+3x</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+8x</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+12</text></g></svg>
caption: The two middle cells, 3x and 8x, multiply to 24x²: the same as the shaded corners, 2x² × 12.

md: For $x^2+7x+12$ you find two numbers that multiply to $12$ and add to $7$. With a number in front of $x^2$ the pair changes: for $ax^2+bx+c$ it must multiply to $ac$ and add to $b$. Split the middle term with that pair, then factorise the four terms in twos.
The grid shows why: its two middle cells always multiply to the same as its two corner cells.

steps.decision: Write ac down first: that single product is what changes when a is not 1.
List the factor pairs of 18 (1 and 18, 2 and 9, 3 and 6) and take the one that adds to 11.
Split 11x as 9x + 2x, then take a common factor from each pair. The two brackets match, which says the pair was right.
Take out the matching bracket. Check the middle: 3x × 3 = 9x and 2 × x = 2x, which add to 11x.

title: Factorising quadratics 2
why: The same split-and-group method on more quadratics with a number in front of x², at writing speed. Watch it once, then answer the checks without going back.

explain: $ac$ is the $x^2$ coefficient times the constant: $2 \times 6 = 12$, as step 1 of See it multiplied $3 \times 6$. The pair you then want multiplies to $12$ and adds to $7$: $4$ and $3$.

twin.explain: $5 \times 6 = 30$; the pair then multiplies to $30$ and adds to $13$: $10$ and $3$.

prompt: Which pair splits the middle term of $5x^2+17x+6$?
explain: The pair multiplies to $ac = 5 \times 6 = 30$ and adds to $17$, as step 2 of See it listed the pairs of $18$: $15 \times 2 = 30$ and $15 + 2 = 17$. A pair built from $6$ alone ignores the $5$.

optionNotes.why: They multiply to 6, the constant, which is the rule only when there is no number in front of x². Here the pair must multiply to 5 × 6 = 30.
They do multiply to 30, but they add to 13, not 17. Both conditions have to hold: product ac and sum b.

twin.prompt: Which pair splits the middle term of $4x^2+13x+3$?
twin.explain: The pair multiplies to $4 \times 3 = 12$ and adds to $13$: $12$ and $1$.

optionNotes.why: They multiply to 3, the constant alone. With 4 in front of x² the pair must multiply to 4 × 3 = 12.
They multiply to 12 but add to 8, not 13; the pair needs both the product and the sum.

text: Why the pair multiplies to ac

alt: A two by two grid with columns headed qx and +n and rows headed px and +m. The cells hold pqx², pnx, mqx and mn; the corner cells pqx² and mn are shaded.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (px + m)(qx + n)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">qx</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+n</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">px</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+m</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">pqx²</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">pnx</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">mqx</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">mn</text></g></svg>
caption: Corners multiply to pq × mn = ac; the middle cells pn and mq multiply to the same.

title: The corners and the middle
md: Expanding $(px+m)(qx+n)$ fills four cells: $pqx^2$, $pnx$, $mqx$ and $mn$. The corners give $a = pq$ and $c = mn$. The middle cells give $b$'s two pieces, $pn$ and $mq$, and $pn \times mq$ is the same four letters as $pq \times mn$. So the pieces of $b$ always multiply to $ac$.
The same grid is the quickest check on any answer: multiply the outer and the inner terms of your brackets and add; the total must be the middle term.

stem: Show that the two pieces of the middle term of $(px+m)(qx+n)$ multiply to $ac$.

steps.decision: Multiply every term in one bracket by every term in the other: four cells of the grid.
Read off the coefficients: the middle term is made of two pieces.
The same four letters, multiplied in another order.

steps.working: So the pair that splits $b$ multiplies to $ac$.
steps.decision: That is why the rule works for every quadratic, and why c alone only works when a is 1.

title: Why Splitting the Middle Works
why: The same argument with the grid, spoken through. Watch it after the steps above, then try the check.

prompt: $4x^2+8x+3 = (2x+1)(2x+3)$, and its middle term splits as $2x + 6x$. What do $2$ and $6$ multiply to?
explain: The two pieces of the middle term multiply to $ac$, as step 3 of See it showed with letters: here $2 \times 6 = 12 = 4 \times 3$. They add to $b$, $8$; they multiply to $ac$, never to $c$ alone.

optionNotes.why: The constant is c alone, which is the product only when a is 1. Here a is 4, so the pieces multiply to 4 × 3 = 12.
8 is what the two pieces add to, not what they multiply to: 2 + 6 = 8 and 2 × 6 = 12.

twin.prompt: $6x^2+7x+2 = (2x+1)(3x+2)$, and its middle term splits as $4x + 3x$. What do $4$ and $3$ multiply to?
twin.explain: The pieces of the middle term multiply to $ac = 6 \times 2 = 12$ and add to $b = 7$.

optionNotes.why: The constant alone is the product only when there is no number in front of x²; here the pieces multiply to 6 × 2 = 12.
7 is the sum of the pieces, 4 + 3; their product is 12.

text: Negative terms: let the pair carry the signs

alt: A two by two grid with columns headed 3x and −5 and rows headed 2x and +3. The cells hold 6x², −10x, +9x and −15; the corner cells are shaded.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (2x + 3)(3x − 5)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3x</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−5</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+3</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">6x²</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−10x</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+9x</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−15</text></g></svg>
caption: A negative c makes one middle cell negative: −10x and +9x add to −x and multiply to −90x² = 6x² × (−15).

md: When $c$ is negative, $ac$ is negative, so the pair has one negative number: look for two factors of $|ac|$ that differ by $b$. When $b$ is negative and $c$ positive, both numbers are negative.
Grouping then needs care: take a negative common factor from the second pair when that is what makes the two brackets match.

steps.working: $ac = 30$ and $b = -11$, so both numbers are negative: $-6$ and $-5$
steps.decision: Product +30 and sum −11: two negatives, from the pairs of 30.
Split −11x as −6x − 5x.
Taking −1 from the second pair, not +1, is what makes its bracket match (5x − 3).
Check the middle: 2x × (−3) + (−1) × 5x = −6x − 5x = −11x.

prompt: The pair for $4x^2-4x-3$ multiplies to $-12$ and adds to $-4$. Which pair?
explain: A negative product means one number is negative, and a negative sum means the larger one is: $-6 \times 2 = -12$ and $-6 + 2 = -4$, the sign rule step 1 of See it used.

optionNotes.why: The product is right, but 6 + (−2) = +4. The sum must be −4, so the larger number takes the minus sign.
They multiply to −3, the constant alone; the pair must multiply to ac = 4 × (−3) = −12.

twin.prompt: The pair for $3x^2+4x-4$ multiplies to $-12$ and adds to $4$. Which pair?
twin.explain: One number is negative, and the sum is positive, so the larger is positive: $6 \times (-2) = -12$ and $6 + (-2) = 4$.

optionNotes.why: The product is right but the sum is −4; the sum must be +4, so the larger number is the positive one.
They multiply to −4, the constant alone; the pair must multiply to 3 × (−4) = −12.

md: Before looking for a pair, take out the highest common factor of every term, numbers and letters together. It makes the numbers smaller, and a factor left inside a bracket costs the last mark: "fully" means nothing more comes out of any bracket.
Letters count too: every term of $4ax^2+10ax+6a$ holds $2a$, so $2a$ comes out and the bracket left, $2x^2+5x+3$, is an ordinary quadratic.

steps.decision: 3 divides 6, 3 and 18, so it comes out first.
Work on the bracket with its own a, b and c.
Split and group inside the bracket; the 3 waits outside.
Keep the 3 in the final answer: it is part of the product.

explain: Take out $2$ first, as step 1 of See it took out $3$: $2(2x^2+7x+6)$. Inside, the pair multiplies to $12$ and adds to $7$, $4$ and $3$, giving $2(2x+3)(x+2)$. A bracket with a common factor inside is not fully factorised.

optionNotes.why: It multiplies back correctly, but 4x + 6 still has a common factor of 2, so it is not fully factorised: take the 2 out.
Expand it: 2(2x² + 8x + 6) = 4x² + 16x + 12, not 14x. The pair inside must add to 7: 4 and 3.

twin.explain: Take out $3$: $3(2x^2+5x+3)$, then the pair $3$ and $2$ gives $3(2x+3)(x+1)$.

optionNotes.why: 6x + 9 still has a common factor of 3; take it out to finish.
Expanding gives 3(2x² + 7x + 3) = 6x² + 21x + 9, not 15x; check the middle term before you stop.

text: A difference of two squares in disguise

alt: On the left, a square of side a with a smaller square of side b cut from one corner, leaving an L-shape labelled a² − b². On the right, the same area rearranged as a rectangle a + b long and a − b wide, labelled (a + b)(a − b).
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 200" width="330" height="200" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>A square with a smaller square cut away, and the same area as a rectangle</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><path d="M30 44H122V100H86V136H30Z" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="86" y="100" width="36" height="36" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><rect x="196" y="64" width="128" height="56" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="76" y="34" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a</text><text x="22" y="95" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a</text><text x="104" y="154" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b</text><text x="260" y="56" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a + b</text><text x="188" y="97" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a − b</text><text x="76" y="188" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a² − b²</text><text x="260" y="150" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">(a + b)(a − b)</text></g></svg>
caption: Cut b² from a²; the L-shape that is left rearranges into a rectangle (a + b) by (a − b).

md: $a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b)$ for any $a$ and $b$. After a common factor comes out, what is left is often a square minus a square with numbers in front: $9x^2 = (3x)^2$ and $4y^2 = (2y)^2$. A middle term means it is not a difference of two squares: $4x^2-12x+9$ is the square $(2x-3)^2$.

steps.decision: The highest common factor of 18 and 8 is 2; the letters share nothing.
Write each term as something squared: the bracket is a square minus a square.
Apply a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), keeping the 2 outside.

explain: Take out $3$, then $9p^2-4q^2$ is $(3p)^2-(2q)^2$, a difference of two squares, as step 2 of See it rewrote $9x^2-4y^2$. "Fully" means finishing it: $3(3p+2q)(3p-2q)$.

optionNotes.why: The common factor is right and earns its mark, but the bracket is still a square minus a square, so it is not fully factorised.
A squared bracket has a middle term when expanded, −12pq; this expression has none, so it is (3p + 2q)(3p − 2q).
The common factor is out, but the bracket is a difference of two squares that still factorises.
It multiplies back correctly, but 10m + 4n still has a factor of 2: take it out to finish.

text: Fractions and products can be squares

md: A fraction is a square when its top and bottom are: $\frac{9}{25}x^2 = \left(\frac{3}{5}x\right)^2$, because $\sqrt{9} = 3$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$. A product of letters can be a square too: $16x^2y^2 = (4xy)^2$. Most candidates scored nothing on a fraction like this in Summer 2023, only because they did not look for the square root.

steps.decision: Square-root the top and the bottom of the fraction separately.
Apply a² − b² with a = 3x/5 and b = 2.

steps.working: Check: $\frac{3}{5}x \times \frac{3}{5}x = \frac{9}{25}x^2$ and the middle terms cancel
steps.decision: Expanding back is the fastest check that nothing was lost.

explain: $\frac{1}{16}x^2 = \left(\frac{1}{4}x\right)^2$ because $\sqrt{1} = 1$ and $\sqrt{16} = 4$, the square root step 1 of See it took; and $9 = 3^2$. So it is $\left(\frac{1}{4}x+3\right)\left(\frac{1}{4}x-3\right)$.

optionNotes.why: Taking 1/16 out leaves x² − 144 inside, not x² − 9, so this does not multiply back to the question.
Its square term is x²/256, not x²/16: the fraction has to be square-rooted, top and bottom.
Taking 4/49 out changes the 1 inside: this multiplies back to 4x²/49 − 4/49, not the question.
The fraction was not square-rooted: its square is 16x²/2401, not 4x²/49.

alt: A two by two grid with columns headed x and +3y and rows headed 2x and −y. The cells hold 2x², +6xy, −xy and −3y²; the corner cells are shaded.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (2x − y)(x + 3y)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.09"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+3y</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−y</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2x²</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+6xy</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−xy</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−3y²</text></g></svg>
caption: The y rides along in every cell: +6xy and −xy make the middle term +5xy, and the corner −3y² needs y in both brackets.

md: A quadratic in $x$ and $y$ factorises by the same pair: $ac$ and $b$ are the coefficients. The second letter stays beside each number in the brackets, or the $y^2$ term could not appear when you multiply back. Check a two-letter answer that way: the $x^2$, $xy$ and $y^2$ terms must all come back.

steps.decision: Use the coefficients 3, 7 and 2 exactly as in a one-letter quadratic.
Split 7xy as 6xy + xy; the second common factor is y, not 1.
Every bracket keeps its y: multiplying back gives the 2y² term.

explain: The pair multiplies to $8$ and adds to $-6$: $-2$ and $-4$, each carrying a $y$, as step 3 of See it kept its $y$. So $(x-2y)(x-4y)$, which gives $-6xy$ in the middle and $+8y^2$ at the end; without the $y$ there is no $y^2$ term.

optionNotes.why: The numbers are right, but the y was dropped: multiplying back gives x² − 6x + 8, with no y at all.
That gives −2xy in the middle and −8y² at the end; both numbers must be negative to add to −6 and multiply to +8.

twin.explain: Two negatives that multiply to $12$ and add to $-7$: $-3$ and $-4$, each with its $y$.

optionNotes.why: The y was dropped, so the y² term cannot appear when you multiply back.
That gives −xy and −12y²; both numbers must be negative for +12y² and −7xy.

text: Four terms: group them in pairs

alt: A two by two grid with columns headed 2q and −3 and rows headed 2p and +5. The cells hold 4pq, −6p, +10q and −15.
svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 214" width="300" height="214" role="img" font-family="system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Arial, sans-serif"><title>Area grid for (2p + 5)(2q − 3)</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"><rect x="78" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="44" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="78" y="114" width="104" height="70"/><rect x="182" y="114" width="104" height="70"/></g><g><text x="130" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2q</text><text x="234" y="30" font-size="16" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−3</text><text x="64" y="85" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2p</text><text x="64" y="155" font-size="16" text-anchor="end" font-weight="600" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+5</text><text x="130" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4pq</text><text x="234" y="85" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−6p</text><text x="130" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">+10q</text><text x="234" y="155" font-size="17" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−15</text></g></svg>
caption: Four unlike terms are already the four cells: each row shares a factor, and so does each column.

md: Four terms with no square in sight, such as $4pq-6p+10q-15$, are the four cells of a grid already. Factorise the first pair and the last pair separately; if the two brackets match, take the bracket out. If they differ only in sign, take a negative factor from the second pair.

steps.decision: 3a comes out of the first pair and 4 out of the second; both leave (b − 2).
The matching bracket comes out; what is left, 3a + 4, is the other bracket.
Two of the four products are enough to see the brackets are right.

explain: $2x(y+3)$ from the first pair and $-5(y+3)$ from the second, the negative factor that makes the brackets match, as step 1 of See it matched $(b-2)$. Then the bracket comes out: $(2x-5)(y+3)$.

optionNotes.why: Multiplying back gives +5y + 15, but the question has −5y − 15: the second factor is −5.
This is the right step, but it is still two terms; take the common bracket out to finish.
Multiplying back gives −2n + 8, but the question has +2n − 8: the second factor is +2.
Right so far, but still two terms; the common bracket has to come out.

text: How the paper asks: factorise, then use it

md: The command is bare: "Factorise" or "Factorise fully", 2 or 3 marks, the first for the common factor or the split and the last for the complete product. Every M4 paper from 2018 to 2026 has at least one, and the later one often continues: "Hence simplify" a fraction.

Four losses recur in the reports: stopping after the common factor (November 2025); dividing single terms instead of whole brackets (November 2024, 35% full marks); reordering a difference of two squares so a sign changes (Summer 2025); and missing a fraction's square root (Summer 2023).

steps.decision: Factorise the top: ac = −6, pair 6 and −1.
The bottom is a difference of two squares, (3x)² − 1².
Cancel the whole bracket (3x − 1), never single terms like 3x² and 9x².

explain: Factorise both lines first, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did: $(2x-1)(x+3)$ over $(2x+1)(2x-1)$. The whole bracket $(2x-1)$ cancels, leaving $\frac{x+3}{2x+1}$. Cancelling single terms such as $2x^2$ with $4x^2$ is never allowed.

optionNotes.why: The top's brackets are (2x − 1)(x + 3): multiplying back gives +5x only with +3, so the sign of 3 is positive.
That cancels 2x² against 4x² term by term, which changes the value. Factorise both lines and cancel a whole bracket.
The top is (3x − 1)(x − 2); a +2 would make its middle term +5x, not −7x.
Terms were cancelled one by one; only a whole bracket common to top and bottom can cancel.

text: Going further: a bracket as the letter

md: The hardest versions put a whole bracket where a letter would be: $(4n+3)^2-(3n+4)^2$ in Summer 2022, $(x-2)^2+5(x-2)$ in January 2019. Treat the bracket as one letter: a square minus a square is still $(a+b)(a-b)$, and a repeated bracket is still a common factor. Then tidy each new bracket.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Completing the square is excluded at M4 by the Teacher Guidance, and cubics and the factor theorem are A level. Solving by factorising is M3; here you factorise, and the paper then asks you to use it.

steps.decision: a = 3n + 2 and b = 2n + 3: the difference of two squares with brackets for letters.
Collect each bracket; the minus in front of (2n + 3) changes both of its signs.
Fully: 5n + 5 still has a factor of 5.

explain: $(y+3)$ is in both terms, so it comes out, as step 1 of See it treated a bracket as one letter: $(y+3)[(y+3)-4] = (y+3)(y-1)$. The inner bracket is $y + 3 - 4$, not $y - 4$.

optionNotes.why: What is left after taking out (y + 3) is (y + 3) − 4, which collects to y − 1; the +3 was dropped.
That is the expression multiplied out, so it is not factorised: the answer has to be a product.
The bracket left is (x − 1) + 3, which collects to x + 2; the −1 was dropped.
That is multiplied out; factorising means leaving it as a product.

md: The difference of two squares is one expansion read backwards. Multiply $(a+b)(a-b)$ and the two middle terms cancel, which is why a difference of two squares has no middle term, and why a quadratic that has one is not a difference of two squares.

steps.decision: Multiply each term of the first bracket by each term of the second.
The two middle terms are opposites, so they cancel.
Only the two squares remain: read backwards, that is the factorisation.

prompt: Why does $(a+b)(a-b)$ have no middle term?
options: a and b are never multiplied
explain: Expanding gives $-ab$ from $a \times (-b)$ and $+ab$ from $b \times a$, as step 2 of See it showed: equal and opposite, so they cancel. Only $a^2$ and $-b^2$ are left.

optionNotes.option: a and b are never multiplied
optionNotes.why: They are multiplied twice, a × (−b) and b × a; the two products cancel each other.
b² is a separate term and stays in the answer; the middle terms cancel with each other.
The middle terms, −14x and +14x, cancel; they do not add to −28x.
7 × (−7) = −49, so the last term is negative.

Find the pair that multiplies to $ac$ and adds to $b$, and split the middle term.
Group four terms in pairs, choosing the sign that makes the brackets match.
Take out the highest common factor first, letters included, and finish every bracket.
Factorise a difference of two squares when the squares are fractions, products or brackets.
Keep the second letter in both brackets of a two-letter quadratic.

Every M4 paper asks at least once, for 2 or 3 marks, and the later question often goes on to "Hence simplify". The first mark is the common factor or the split; the last is the complete product with nothing left to take out. Stuck: write $ac$ down and list its pairs, and expand your answer's middle term to check it.
